items.stem: When summarising an ethnography for IB Paper 2, which details establish its context?
items.answer: The author, the people studied, the place and the time of the fieldwork
items.markingKey: The author, the people studied, the place and the time of the fieldwork. Context means who, where and when, plus the wider setting.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "An ethnography is simply a neutral description of a culture." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: An ethnography is an argued interpretation shaped by the author's question, methods, theory and position.
items.markingKey: An ethnography is an argued interpretation shaped by the author's question, methods, theory and position. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why it is important to identify an ethnographer's research question.
items.answer: The question determines what the ethnographer looked for, which methods they used and what they may have overlooked, so it helps readers evaluate the evidence and compare ethnographies fairly. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The question determines what the ethnographer looked for, which methods they used and what they may have overlooked, so it helps readers evaluate the evidence and compare ethnographies fairly. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I spent eighteen months on night shifts at the delivery depot, sorting parcels and later riding with drivers. My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. If I join the union, my cousin's company won't give me shifts." I recorded 46 interviews and kept a diary of the shifts I worked. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): from the introduction to an ethnography of delivery drivers in Berlin.

Using evidence from the text, describe the research question, methods and argument presented in the text. Organise your answer as a series of clearly separated descriptive points.
items.answer: Question: why drivers who complain about the algorithm refuse to join the union. Methods: eighteen months of night-shift participant observation (sorting parcels, riding with drivers), 46 interviews, a diary of shifts. Argument: drivers experience the platform as both control and a space of self-employment they are reluctant to give up.
items.markingKey: Question: why drivers who complain about the algorithm refuse to join the union. Methods: eighteen months of night-shift participant observation (sorting parcels, riding with drivers), 46 interviews, a diary of shifts. Argument: drivers experience the platform as both control and a space of self-employment they are reluctant to give up. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Briefly describe Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping and explain what it reveals about the relationship between research question, evidence and argument.
items.answer: Drawing on work in the Alto do Cruzeiro over decades, she argued that chronic scarcity shaped mothers' responses to infant death and that hunger was medicalised as nervos. Her question about maternal love and infant death led her to collect reproductive histories and observe clinics, and the evidence supports her contested argument about everyday violence.
items.markingKey: Context (Drawing on work in the Alto do Cruzeiro over decades, she argued that chronic scarcity shaped mothers' responses to infant death and that hunger was medicalised as nervos.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: her question about maternal love and infant death led her to collect reproductive histories and observe clinics, and the evidence supports her contested argument about everyday violence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the relationship between research question, evidence and argument.

Read the text below.

My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. If I join the union, my cousin's company won't give me shifts." I recorded 46 interviews and kept a diary of the shifts I worked. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): from the introduction to an ethnography of delivery drivers in Berlin.

Explain how the anthropologist's methods support the argument in the text, using one or more anthropological concepts. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: Long-term participant observation in the same shifts shows the work from within and builds rapport (Kemal's frank answer); interviews give drivers' own explanations; Kemal's statement directly illustrates the ambivalence (control/freedom) and reveals kinship ties (cousin's company) that shape decisions – evidence for the argument that platform power is experienced ambivalently.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Long-term participant observation in the same shifts shows the work from within and builds rapport (Kemal's frank answer); interviews give drivers' own explanations; Kemal's statement directly illustrates the ambivalence (control/freedom) and reveals kinship ties (cousin's company) that shape decisions – evidence for the argument that platform power is experienced ambivalently. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "An ethnography written decades ago has little value for understanding the present."
items.answer: Older ethnographies remain valuable if situated in their time and read critically.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: societies have changed, so old accounts may mislead; theories and ethics of the time may be outdated. Arguments against: it is a historical record that allows study of change (Weiner's restudy of Malinowski); its arguments may still illuminate concepts. Supported judgement: Older ethnographies remain valuable if situated in their time and read critically.

items.stem: Using Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping and Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies, compare the ways in which power is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)): She describes the "everyday violence" of poverty, in which hunger is medicalised as nervos and treated with tranquillisers and vitamins, hiding the political causes of suffering. Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)): She describes the "everyday violence" of poverty, in which hunger is medicalised as nervos and treated with tranquillisers and vitamins, hiding the political causes of suffering. Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes uses Bourdieu's idea of symbolic violence to show how this hierarchy is naturalised: supervisors, doctors and sometimes workers themselves explain Triqui suffering by their bodies or culture rather than by labour conditions. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why an ethnography's argument must be distinguished from its description.
items.answer: Description reports what was observed; the argument is the interpretation the author builds, often contested, so separating them lets a reader assess whether the evidence supports the conclusions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Description reports what was observed; the argument is the interpretation the author builds, often contested, so separating them lets a reader assess whether the evidence supports the conclusions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.markingKey: Award marks for: The question determines what the ethnographer looked for, which methods they used and what they may have overlooked, so it helps readers evaluate the evidence and compare ethnographies fairly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between ethnographic argument and ethnographic description.
items.answer: Description records people, events and practices observed; argument interprets them to make a claim, e.g. that nervos medicalises hunger (Scheper-Hughes).
items.markingKey: Description records people, events and practices observed; argument interprets them to make a claim, e.g. that nervos medicalises hunger (Scheper-Hughes). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline illustrates the concept of identity. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Factory women negotiated identities between village (kampung) norms, consumer modernity and religious expectations of modesty.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Factory women negotiated identities between village (kampung) norms, consumer modernity and religious expectations of modesty. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Aihwa Ong, Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline: Factory Women in Malaysia (1987), among young Malay women working in Japanese-owned electronics factories in Kuala Langat, Selangor, Malaysia (late 1970s)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that an ethnography written decades ago has little value for understanding the present? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Older ethnographies remain valuable if situated in their time and read critically.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: societies have changed, so old accounts may mislead; theories and ethics of the time may be outdated; it is a historical record that allows study of change (Weiner's restudy of Malinowski); its arguments may still illuminate concepts. Suitable ethnographies include Bourgois's In Search of Respect, Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Older ethnographies remain valuable if situated in their time and read critically. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

Read the text below.

I spent eighteen months on night shifts at the delivery depot, sorting parcels and later riding with drivers. My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Consider the obligations owed to different people involved in the research.
items.answer: Drivers risk losing shifts if identified as critical; Kemal's comment about his cousin's company is sensitive; the anthropologist worked for the depot, so the employer's role in consent and confidentiality must be clarified; data from 46 interviews must be stored securely. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Drivers risk losing shifts if identified as critical; Kemal's comment about his cousin's company is sensitive; the anthropologist worked for the depot, so the employer's role in consent and confidentiality must be clarified; data from 46 interviews must be stored securely. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Derek Freeman's critique of Margaret Mead (1983) partly rested on the claim that:
items.answer: Mead's young informants had been joking with her
items.markingKey: Mead's young informants had been joking with her. Freeman argued she was misled; the claim is itself disputed.

items.stem: "Theory is something added after fieldwork is finished." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Theory shapes the research question, what is observed and how notes are taken; it interacts with fieldwork throughout.
items.markingKey: Theory shapes the research question, what is observed and how notes are taken; it interacts with fieldwork throughout. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the ethnographic present and a historically situated account.
items.answer: The ethnographic present describes a society in the present tense as if timeless; a historically situated account specifies dates and context and recognises change.
items.markingKey: The ethnographic present describes a society in the present tense as if timeless; a historically situated account specifies dates and context and recognises change. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify one way in which culture matters in Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Margaret Mead, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to culture. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When I arrived in Mutare in 2009, the shops had no prices: the Zimbabwe dollar had just been abandoned, and people paid in US dollars, South African rand and, for small amounts, sweets. My earlier fieldwork in 1998 had described weekly savings clubs among market women as "rotating and stable". Now Mai Chipo told me the club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt "with new rules, and only women we can see every day". I realise that my first book wrote about the clubs as though they had always existed and always would.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a market town in Zimbabwe.

Identify and describe how the savings clubs had changed between the two periods of fieldwork. Refer closely to the text. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: In 1998 the clubs were described as rotating and stable; by 2009 Mai Chipo's club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt; the new club has new rules and includes only women members see every day; the economic context had changed (abandonment of the Zimbabwe dollar, multiple currencies, sweets as change).
items.markingKey: In 1998 the clubs were described as rotating and stable; by 2009 Mai Chipo's club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt; the new club has new rules and includes only women members see every day; the economic context had changed (abandonment of the Zimbabwe dollar, multiple currencies, sweets as change). Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

Read the text below.

When I arrived in Mutare in 2009, the shops had no prices: the Zimbabwe dollar had just been abandoned, and people paid in US dollars, South African rand and, for small amounts, sweets. My earlier fieldwork in 1998 had described weekly savings clubs among market women as "rotating and stable". Now Mai Chipo told me the club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt "with new rules, and only women we can see every day". I realise that my first book wrote about the clubs as though they had always existed and always would.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a market town in Zimbabwe.

Explain, with close reference to the text, what the text shows about the importance of situating an ethnography in time. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: The anthropologist's first book used the ethnographic present, portraying the clubs as timeless; returning after hyperinflation reveals change driven by economic crisis, and new rules show people adapting social relations (trust limited to those seen daily). Situating the account in time (1998 vs 2009) and context avoids presenting a snapshot as permanent.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The anthropologist's first book used the ethnographic present, portraying the clubs as timeless; returning after hyperinflation reveals change driven by economic crisis, and new rules show people adapting social relations (trust limited to those seen daily). Situating the account in time (1998 vs 2009) and context avoids presenting a snapshot as permanent. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Define the term "ethnographic present".
items.answer: The convention of writing about a society in the present tense, which can make it seem timeless and unchanging
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the convention of writing about a society in the present tense, which can make it seem timeless and unchanging. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the theoretical approach of an ethnography should be identified.
items.answer: Theory directs attention: a functionalist will look for how institutions maintain order, a feminist for gendered power, a political economist for global inequality; knowing the approach helps evaluate and compare accounts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Theory directs attention: a functionalist will look for how institutions maintain order, a feminist for gendered power, a political economist for global inequality; knowing the approach helps evaluate and compare accounts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Mead–Freeman controversy shows situating ethnographies in time, place and theory.
items.answer: Mead described relaxed Samoan adolescence in 1925–1926; Freeman, who worked in Western Samoa from the 1940s, described rivalry, violence and strict virginity norms. Their differences reflect different islands and decades, different informants (adolescent girls vs. chiefs) and theoretical commitments (cultural determinism vs. biology).
items.markingKey: Context (Mead described relaxed Samoan adolescence in 1925–1926; Freeman, who worked in Western Samoa from the 1940s, described rivalry, violence and strict virginity norms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: their differences reflect different islands and decades, different informants (adolescent girls vs. chiefs) and theoretical commitments (cultural determinism vs. biology). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to situating ethnographies in time, place and theory.

items.stem: With reference to E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer (1940), explain how the key concept of space, place and time helps us to understand the changing contexts of ethnographic research.
items.answer: Nuer "oecological time" follows seasonal movement between wet-season villages and dry-season cattle camps, while "structural time" is reckoned by distances between age-sets and lineages.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Nuer "oecological time" follows seasonal movement between wet-season villages and dry-season cattle camps, while "structural time" is reckoned by distances between age-sets and lineages. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer (1940), among Nuer cattle pastoralists of the Upper Nile, southern Sudan (fieldwork 1930–1936)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to space, place and time. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "Restudies are the best way to evaluate an ethnography." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Restudies are valuable but must themselves be situated; they complement rather than replace critical reading.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they reveal change and correct earlier bias (Weiner); they test claims empirically. Arguments against: the society will have changed, so differences may not show earlier error; restudies have their own biases; internal critique of evidence and method is also important. Supported judgement: Restudies are valuable but must themselves be situated; they complement rather than replace critical reading. Markbands (15 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Define the term "generalisation".
items.answer: A broader claim derived from comparing several cases, such as "the less powerful often resist through hidden means"
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a broader claim derived from comparing several cases, such as "the less powerful often resist through hidden means". Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a contrast and a comparison.
items.answer: A comparison identifies similarities between cases; a contrast identifies differences. IB "compare and contrast" questions require both, linked explicitly.
items.markingKey: A comparison identifies similarities between cases; a contrast identifies differences. IB "compare and contrast" questions require both, linked explicitly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why comparison must consider differences in method and theory as well as content.
items.answer: Differences between ethnographies may result from how they were researched and theorised rather than from the societies; recognising this avoids false conclusions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Differences between ethnographies may result from how they were researched and theorised rather than from the societies; recognising this avoids false conclusions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)) as your example, describe how identity is shown.
items.answer: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "A comparison is complete if both ethnographies are described in detail." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Description alone is not comparison; the answer must explicitly identify and explain similarities and differences.
items.markingKey: Description alone is not comparison; the answer must explicitly identify and explain similarities and differences. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Comparing ethnographies from very different societies produces superficial conclusions." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Comparison across difference is valuable when context is explained and concepts are used carefully.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: contexts differ so much that similarities may be misleading; concepts may mean different things in each; shared concepts (power, identity) allow meaningful comparison; difference itself is illuminating; Bourgois–Holmes or Scott–Ong comparisons reveal general processes. Suitable ethnographies include Bourgois's In Search of Respect, Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies, Scott's Weapons of the Weak. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Comparison across difference is valuable when context is explained and concepts are used carefully. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The systematic examination of similarities and differences between practices in different societies to understand a concept or test a generalisation"?
options: interlocutor
restudy
cross-cultural comparison
historical context
items.answer: cross-cultural comparison
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of cross-cultural comparison.

items.stem: Briefly explain why comparing two ethnographies can deepen understanding of a key concept.
items.answer: Seeing a concept such as power operate differently in two contexts shows which features are general and which depend on local conditions, refining the concept and avoiding generalising from one case.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Seeing a concept such as power operate differently in two contexts shows which features are general and which depend on local conditions, refining the concept and avoiding generalising from one case. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which a comparison of Scott and Ong shows everyday forms of resistance.
items.answer: Scott's Malay peasants resist through gossip and foot-dragging; Ong's Malay factory women resist through spirit possession. Both show hidden resistance by the less powerful in Malaysia, but one is rural class conflict over mechanisation and the other gendered resistance to factory discipline expressed in spiritual idioms.
items.markingKey: Context (Scott's Malay peasants resist through gossip and foot-dragging; Ong's Malay factory women resist through spirit possession.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: both show hidden resistance by the less powerful in Malaysia, but one is rural class conflict over mechanisation and the other gendered resistance to factory discipline expressed in spiritual idioms. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to everyday forms of resistance.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

On the tea estate, the women pluckers sing while they work. The supervisor, Mr Perera, says the songs "keep the rhythm and the quota". Kamala translated one for me: "Leaves for the master's cup / Our hands are green, his hands are clean." When the manager walks past, they switch to a hymn. Kamala's daughter will not work on the estate; she studies nursing in Colombo. "My mother sings," she says. "I will speak."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a tea estate in the highlands of Sri Lanka.

Identify and describe the singing practices of the tea pluckers. Refer closely to the text. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: Women sing while plucking; the supervisor believes songs keep the rhythm and the quota; one song contrasts the workers' green hands with the master's clean hands; they switch to a hymn when the manager passes; Kamala's daughter refuses estate work and studies nursing.
items.markingKey: Women sing while plucking; the supervisor believes songs keep the rhythm and the quota; one song contrasts the workers' green hands with the master's clean hands; they switch to a hymn when the manager passes; Kamala's daughter refuses estate work and studies nursing. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evidence"?
options: The observations, quotations, case histories, images and other data an ethnographer uses to support the argument
The location – or set of connected locations – in which ethnographic research is carried out
A broader claim derived from comparing several cases, such as "the less powerful often resist through hidden means"
A specific concept, practice or question (e.g. how resistance is expressed) that is used to compare two ethnographies
items.answer: The observations, quotations, case histories, images and other data an ethnographer uses to support the argument
items.markingKey: A. "evidence" is the observations, quotations, case histories, images and other data an ethnographer uses to support the argument.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "theoretical approach"?
options: The observations, quotations, case histories, images and other data an ethnographer uses to support the argument
Fred Eggan's (1954) method of comparing societies that share history or region so that differences can be linked to specific variables
A broader claim derived from comparing several cases, such as "the less powerful often resist through hidden means"
The framework of ideas (e.g. functionalism, interpretive, political economy, feminist) that shapes the questions an ethnographer asks and how evidence is interpreted
items.answer: The framework of ideas (e.g. functionalism, interpretive, political economy, feminist) that shapes the questions an ethnographer asks and how evidence is interpreted
items.markingKey: D. "theoretical approach" is the framework of ideas (e.g. functionalism, interpretive, political economy, feminist) that shapes the questions an ethnographer asks and how evidence is interpreted.

items.stem: Which pair of ethnographies could be compared on the theme of everyday resistance?
options: Boas on head form and Rivers on genealogies
Augé's Non-Places and Douglas's Purity and Danger
Morgan's Ancient Society and Tylor's Primitive Culture

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Knowing the date of fieldwork does not matter for understanding an ethnography." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Dates matter because societies change and because the theoretical debates of the time shape the analysis; Mead's 1920s Samoa is not Samoa today.

items.stem: Freya writes: "If two ethnographies of the same society disagree, one of them must be wrong." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Differences can reflect change over time, different questions, theories, positionality and informants; both may be partial truths.

items.stem: Distinguish between a comparative study and a restudy.
items.answer: A restudy returns to the same people or place to examine change or an earlier account; a comparative study sets different societies side by side to identify similarities and differences.

items.stem: Distinguish between an integrated comparison and a sequential (end-on) comparison.
items.answer: An integrated comparison discusses both cases together point by point; a sequential comparison describes one case and then the other, leaving links implicit and usually scoring lower.

Read the text below.

I spent eighteen months on night shifts at the delivery depot, sorting parcels and later riding with drivers. My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. If I join the union, my cousin's company won't give me shifts." I recorded 46 interviews and kept a diary of the shifts I worked. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): from the introduction to an ethnography of delivery drivers in Berlin.

Analyse how the anthropologist's methods support the argument in the text. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Long-term participant observation in the same shifts shows the work from within and builds rapport (Kemal's frank answer); interviews give drivers' own explanations; Kemal's statement directly illustrates the ambivalence (control/freedom) and reveals kinship ties (cousin's company) that shape decisions – evidence for the argument that platform power is experienced ambivalently.

items.stem: Briefly describe Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer (1940) and explain what it reveals about the importance of historical context.
items.answer: The fieldwork took place in the 1930s, shortly after British punitive campaigns against the Nuer, and the account is written largely in the ethnographic present. The colonial situation shaped Nuer suspicion of the anthropologist and his access, yet the text presents Nuer society as a timeless system.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

On the tea estate, the women pluckers sing while they work. The supervisor, Mr Perera, says the songs "keep the rhythm and the quota". Kamala translated one for me: "Leaves for the master's cup / Our hands are green, his hands are clean." When the manager walks past, they switch to a hymn. Kamala's daughter will not work on the estate; she studies nursing in Colombo. "My mother sings," she says. "I will speak."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a tea estate in the highlands of Sri Lanka.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the songs can be understood as a form of resistance. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: The songs carry hidden criticism of inequality ("our hands are green, his hands are clean") understood by workers but not by supervisors, who see only productivity; switching to a hymn conceals the critique from the manager – a hidden transcript of the less powerful. The daughter's "I will speak" points to change from hidden to open resistance through education and mobility.

items.stem: With reference to Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, explain how it illustrates the relationship between research question, evidence and argument.
items.answer: Drawing on work in the Alto do Cruzeiro over decades, she argued that chronic scarcity shaped mothers' responses to infant death and that hunger was medicalised as nervos. Her question about maternal love and infant death led her to collect reproductive histories and observe clinics, and the evidence supports her contested argument about everyday violence.

When I arrived in Mutare in 2009, the shops had no prices: the Zimbabwe dollar had just been abandoned, and people paid in US dollars, South African rand and, for small amounts, sweets. My earlier fieldwork in 1998 had described weekly savings clubs among market women as "rotating and stable". Now Mai Chipo told me the club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt "with new rules, and only women we can see every day". I realise that my first book wrote about the clubs as though they had always existed and always would.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a market town in Zimbabwe.

Describe how the savings clubs had changed between the two periods of fieldwork, as presented in the text. Refer to at least three specific details from the text.
items.answer: In 1998 the clubs were described as rotating and stable; by 2009 Mai Chipo's club had collapsed twice and been rebuilt; the new club has new rules and includes only women members see every day; the economic context had changed (abandonment of the Zimbabwe dollar, multiple currencies, sweets as change).

items.stem: Explain how Bourgois's In Search of Respect illustrates the concept of identity. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that restudies are the best way to evaluate an ethnography? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Restudies are valuable but must themselves be situated; they complement rather than replace critical reading.

items.stem: "Comparing ethnographies from very different societies produces superficial conclusions." Discuss.
items.answer: Comparison across difference is valuable when context is explained and concepts are used carefully.

items.stem: Briefly describe a comparison of Bourgois and Holmes and explain what it reveals about comparing ethnographies through a shared concept.

items.stem: Compare and contrast Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline and Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments as accounts of similar processes in different societies, focusing on the key concept of power.
items.answer: Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline (among young Malay women working in Japanese-owned electronics factories in Kuala Langat, Selangor, Malaysia (late 1970s)): Episodes of spirit possession on the shop floor halted production; Ong interprets them as protest against the strict time discipline and male supervision of factory work. Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments (among the Awlad 'Ali Bedouin of Egypt's Western Desert (fieldwork from 1978)): Women and young men – those with less power – express love, loss and vulnerability through short ghinnawa poems, a socially acceptable channel for sentiments that would breach the honour code if spoken directly. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

I spent eighteen months on night shifts at the delivery depot, sorting parcels and later riding with drivers. My question was simple: why do drivers who complain constantly about the app's algorithm refuse to join the union? Kemal laughed when I asked. "The app is my boss, but the app is also my freedom. If I join the union, my cousin's company won't give me shifts." I recorded 46 interviews and kept a diary of the shifts I worked. I argue that drivers experience the platform not only as control but as a space of self-employment that they are reluctant to give up.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): from the introduction to an ethnography of delivery drivers in Berlin.

Compare and contrast how power is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995)). Refer to specific evidence from both the text and the ethnography.
items.answer: Text: Long-term participant observation in the same shifts shows the work from within and builds rapport (Kemal's frank answer); interviews give drivers' own explanations; Kemal's statement directly illustrates the ambivalence (control/freedom) and reveals kinship ties (cousin's company) that shape decisions – evidence for the argument that platform power is experienced ambivalently. Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how social relations is shown in Clifford Geertz, "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" (1972; reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973) and E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer (1940).
items.answer: Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)): Men bet on the cocks of their own kin group or village and never against them, so patterns of betting map kinship, alliance and rivalry. Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer (among Nuer cattle pastoralists of the Upper Nile, southern Sudan (fieldwork 1930–1936)): Political order rested on segmentary lineages that united against more distant groups and divided when conflict arose within, giving order without a state. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
